newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Russian troops on angry, bitter march home.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Russian troops on angry, bitter march home.

text.p: Two years after they stormed rebel Chechnya in what was to be a quick operation to crush a group of "bandits", Russian troops are in retreat after one of the most shocking defeats in recent military history.
Thousands of Russian soldiers swarmed into the Moslem territory on December 11, 1994, to oust the three-year-old independence-minded regime led by the late Dzhokhar Dudayev.
Moscow said at the time the operation to "restore constitutional order" would be over in days or weeks.
Instead troops ended up bogged down in a brutal conflict in which they never really got the upper hand. Tens of thousands of people were killed in the hugely destructive war.

Now the troops are leaving Chechnya along the same roads their hundreds of tanks and armoured vehicles rolled in on, forced into the humiliating position of asking for Chechen escorts to ensure their safety on the way out.

They are glad to be going home after the government finally abandoned the 21-month war, but many blame Moscow for sending them here in the first place and some say they could have crushed the rebels had they been given proper support.

"We've done our duty and we've nothing to be ashamed of," said Ivan Alekseiivich, a platoon commander giving only his name and patronymic. "Our soldiers just want to go home. That's all anyone talks about," he said in a refrain typical among the troops.
CHECHENS CALL THE SHOTS

The extent of Moscow's humiliation at the hands of the scrappy fighters of a tiny region whose self-declared independence has not been recognised anywhere is visible at the checkpoint Ivan's men help to run along Chechnya's main highway.
Just a few weeks ago only gruff Russian soldiers stood guard here. After a peace agreement was signed in August, it became a joint post and a group of Chechen fighters joined in.
Now there is no mistaking who calls the shots.

The camouflage-clad Chechens, branded as bandits and criminals just weeks ago, joke loudly as they check cars while the Russians huddle meekly behind them in muddy bunkers, venturing out only when neccessary.
An enormous green Chechen flag flies over the scene.
"How are we supposed to feel? We didn't decide to come here on our own, politicians sent us. Now they (the Chechens) are here standing over us," Ivan said resentfully.

Russia's failure to defeat Chechnya, a mountainous strip of land along its southern border containing less than one percent of its population, has raised far-reaching questions about the former superpower's state of military readiness.

Faced with staggering losses and discontent at home, Moscow opted to pull out in exchange for a modest separatist concession to delay discussion of the oil-rich region's constitutional status for five years.
Moscow says all of its soldiers will leave Chechnya by January 25, the eve of presidential and parliamentary elections which are sure to reinforce the grip of the separatists.
Those who remain behind bide their time by dismantling their bunkers and makeshift living quarters.
TROOPS INSIST THEY COULD HAVE WON

Many seem to be in a state of denial over the poor performance of the military, repeating popular but fuzzy conspiracy theories that the country's leaders and top military brass started and lost the war for purely financial reasons.

"Do you think that little Chechnya really defeated great Russia?" said Vitaly, a 23-year old Interior Ministry soldier. "We had more than enough firepower to turn this place to ashes in two days, but everyone was too busy lining their pockets."
Boris, his pot-bellied 40-year-old colleague, said not enough force was used to put down the highly-motivated rebels.
"We should have used old-fashioned Russian might. We should have killed everyone in sight rather than worrying more about women and children than our own lives," he said.

Russian warplanes and artillery did, however, bomb the once-thriving capital Grozny into a smoking ruin before finally capturing it in February 1995, killing thousands of people in the process. Ferocious air bombardments and shelling were also used against villages, without managing to dislodge the rebels.

The Chechens, many of whom regarded the war as just another day of battle in a 300-year struggle to throw off what they see as the Russian colonial yoke, often fought with kamikaze-like abandon that left observers dumbfounded.
They even fashioned homemade anti-aircraft weapons from downed Russian helicopters and heavy guns from the turrets of damaged tanks in place of more conventional arms.
Most of the Russian troops scoff at official casualty figures of around 4,000 dead and more than 1,900 missing.

"There were more soldiers killed here in one year than in 10 years in Afghanistan," said Sasha, a 38-year old captain, referring to the Soviet Union's disastrous Afghan intervention from 1979 to 1989.
Dudayev, a former Soviet Air Force General who came home in 1991 to lead Chechnya's independence movement, was one of those killed. And yet it is he who has the last laugh.

A few days after the Russians marched into his republic, Russian state TV played a tape of Dudayev speaking by telephone to one of his top commanders, aiming to show that the volatile Chechen leader was mad.
"Attack! Retreat! Attack! Retreat!, until they (the Russians) run away in fear," he shouted erratically.
But he also predicted that eventually Moscow would ask for a corridor for its troops to go home.
